voiceover: How soon did the first Christians start proclaiming that Jesus rose from the dead? Astonishingly soon — within a few years of the cross. Here's how we know. Writing around AD 55, the apostle Paul stops and recites a creed he says he did not invent — one he 'received' and 'delivered.' It's 1 Corinthians 15: that Christ died for our sins, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared. And the creed carries its own age. It uses the rabbinic language of received-and-delivered tradition, its wording isn't Paul's usual Greek, and it names Peter by his Aramaic name, Cephas — the marks of a formula older than the letter that quotes it. So count backward. The crucifixion is around AD 30. Within a few years of his conversion, Paul went to Jerusalem and met Peter and James — the very men the creed names as witnesses. That puts the creed within about two to five years of the cross. Even the atheist New Testament scholar Gerd Ludemann dated the tradition to the first two years after the crucifixion. So this wasn't a story that grew over generations. It's the message the apostles were preaching from the very start: Christ died, was buried, rose, and appeared. Early. Sincere. Anchored in named eyewitnesses. The gospel the church proclaimed from the beginning. Not a legend that grew. A claim from the very start.
